title: Judges 3:7–11
context: Othniel’s account is the first and shortest of the judge stories, and it reads almost like a template for the cycle the book has described. Israel does evil and forgets the LORD, the LORD’s anger hands them over to Cushan Rishathaim for eight years, the people cry out, the LORD raises up a savior, his Spirit comes upon that savior, victory follows, and the land has rest for forty years. Othniel is already known from earlier in the story as Caleb’s kinsman who took Kiriath Sepher (Joshua 15:16–17; Judges 1:12–13). Both traditions agree that the passage presents deliverance as the LORD’s work through a human agent he equips, and that the pattern of sin, oppression, cry, and rescue reveals both God’s justice and his mercy toward a wayward people.

verses.text: The children of Israel did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, and forgot the LORD their God, and served the Baals and the Asheroth.
verses.arminianNotes:
The cycle begins: Israel did evil in the LORD’s sight, forgot the LORD their God, and served the Baals and the Asheroth. Forgetting here is not a lapse of memory but a turning away from covenant loyalty.

Arminian readers emphasize that Israel’s forgetting was a culpable act of the will. The people had every reason to remember the LORD’s deeds, and their turning to the Baals was a real rejection of a relationship they were free to keep or abandon.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note how quickly Israel turns from the God who had given them the land, an illustration of the persistent bent of the human heart toward idolatry apart from God’s renewing grace.

Both traditions agree that the evil is defined by reference to the LORD’s sight, that is, by his covenant standard rather than by Israel’s own judgment, and that serving other gods is the root sin from which the book’s other troubles grow.

verses.text: Therefore the LORD’s anger burned against Israel, and he sold them into the hand of Cushan Rishathaim king of Mesopotamia; and the children of Israel served Cushan Rishathaim eight years.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD’s anger burns, and he sells Israel into the hand of Cushan Rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia, for eight years. The language of selling pictures God handing his people over as a consequence of their unfaithfulness.

Arminian readers see the oppression as a just and corrective response to Israel’s choices. God’s anger is not arbitrary but the fitting reaction of a covenant Lord whose people have broken faith, and it aims to bring them back.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that even a foreign king’s conquest is under the LORD’s hand; Cushan Rishathaim is an instrument of God’s discipline, not an independent power. The name may carry a sense like doubly wicked, though its exact meaning and the king’s identity are uncertain.

Both traditions agree that God disciplines his people through historical events and that his anger serves his covenant purposes rather than ending his commitment to Israel.

verses.text: When the children of Israel cried to the LORD, the LORD raised up a savior to the children of Israel, who saved them, even Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother.
verses.arminianNotes:
When Israel cries to the LORD, he raises up a savior, Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother. The cry does not earn the rescue, but the LORD responds to it with mercy.

Arminian readers highlight the responsive character of God in this pattern. He hears the cry of his suffering people and acts in answer to it, showing a God who engages with his people’s turning in real time and in real relationship.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers emphasize that the LORD raised up the savior; the initiative and the provision are his. Israel’s cry is real, but the book never presents it as a deep repentance that merits deliverance, so the rescue displays grace.

Both traditions agree that God’s mercy meets his people in their distress, and that the word savior here points to the LORD’s pattern of rescuing his people through a chosen deliverer.

verses.text: The LORD’s Spirit came on him, and he judged Israel; and he went out to war, and the LORD delivered Cushan Rishathaim king of Mesopotamia into his hand. His hand prevailed against Cushan Rishathaim.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD’s Spirit comes on Othniel, he judges Israel, goes to war, and the LORD delivers Cushan Rishathaim into his hand. Othniel’s victory is credited first to the LORD and then described as his hand prevailing.

Arminian readers see divine empowerment and human action working together. Othniel truly fights and truly judges, and the Spirit’s coming equips him for that task, showing the cooperative way God often works through those he calls.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the Spirit is the decisive factor: the LORD both equips the deliverer and delivers the enemy into his hand. The victory is God’s gift from first to last, even as Othniel acts.

Both traditions agree that the Spirit’s coming in Judges is an empowerment for leadership and deliverance rather than a statement about personal salvation, and that the LORD is the true agent of Israel’s rescue.

verses.text: The land had rest forty years, then Othniel the son of Kenaz died.
verses.arminianNotes:
The land has rest forty years, and then Othniel the son of Kenaz dies. The brief notice closes the model story and hints that the rest lasts only as long as the judge’s lifetime.

Arminian readers note that the peace Israel enjoys is real but fragile, depending on the continued faithfulness of the people. The death of the judge becomes the moment when the people’s own commitment, or lack of it, is exposed again.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see in the limited span of rest a sign that no human judge can bring lasting peace. Each deliverer dies, and the cycle resumes, pointing to Israel’s need for a more enduring rule and a deeper renewal than any judge provides.

Both traditions agree that forty years of rest is a genuine gift from God, and that the pattern of rest followed by renewed failure is central to the message of the book.
